game.name: Enter the Gungeon
game.short_description: Enter the Gungeon is a bullet hell dungeon crawler following a band of misfits seeking to shoot, loot, dodge roll and table-flip their way to personal absolution by reaching the legendary Gungeon’s ultimate treasure: the gun that can kill the past.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Enter the Gungeon is a famous top-down action shooter roguelike that he has played extensively, 100 percent completing it. He calls it a masterpiece and an obvious S tier, and says it helped revive roguelikes alongside Binding of Isaac. He does feel it could offer more content today and he now prefers the more modern-feeling Dead Cells, partly from burnout after so many hours.
praise: Very funny vibe, with references everywhere
Huge number of items and guns, each with quirky effects that are fun to discover
Mix of roguelike power-ups and skill: mastering the mechanics is rewarded with consistent wins
Regular content updates with new bosses and items kept it exciting
Historically important in bringing roguelikes back
criticism: He always wants more out of it; it could have more content
Feels a bit dated and less modern than newer roguelikes
He is getting tired of it after playing it so much
unique_points: Balances roguelike randomness that can make you overpowered with a skill ceiling that rewards mastery
Gun and item discovery with quirky effects drives the fun

design_criteria: Charm/visuals: funny references, cute art and animations
Item and gun diversity: many quirky weapons worth discovering
Skill vs randomness: mastery rewarded alongside overpowered runs
Content depth: wishes it had more
Updates/longevity: new bosses and items over time

community.one_liner: A gun-themed bullet-hell dungeon crawler from Dodge Roll (published by Devolver Digital, 2016) in which quirky Gungeoneers dodge-roll through procedurally generated chambers to reach the gun that can kill the past.
community.consensus_summary: Enter the Gungeon is widely regarded as a genre standard-bearer for action roguelikes. It holds an Overwhelmingly Positive Steam rating (about 95% of roughly 90k reviews) and Metacritic critic scores in the low-to-mid 80s (PC 84, PS4 82, Xbox One 85, Switch 87), with a more lukewarm Metacritic user score of 7.7. Players and critics praise the weapon variety, tight dodge-roll combat, pixel art, theming and humour, and the huge depth of secrets. Complaints centre on its punishing difficulty, heavy RNG, unlock-only (no permanent stat) progression and weak-gun clutter. It is not early access; the last major content patch (A Farewell to Arms, April 2019) ended development, although it reached mobile in 2025 and Steam reviews show players still active in 2026. The sequel Enter the Gungeon 2 has since been announced/released on Steam.
best_things: Huge, whimsical roster of guns and items packed with pop-culture references, and a consistent gun-pun theme (Chambers, Gundead, Blanks, Ammonomicon)
Tight, responsive dodge-roll and bullet-hell combat that rewards skill over stacking overpowered builds
Polished pixel art, music and charm; reviewers say the love for gaming culture is obvious
Enormous endgame of secrets: hidden floors, secret bosses, secret characters and quests that keep players returning for hundreds of hours
Fair-feeling difficulty curve in the eyes of fans: deaths feel earned and improvement is tangible
Local co-op, pause-and-save, free DLC updates and a very low price for the content
Bosses are memorable and distinct, with no-hit bonuses that reward mastery
worst_things: Progression is almost entirely item unlocks; you always restart with the same stats, so meta-progression feels thin compared with Hades-style rogue-lites
Runs are heavily RNG-dependent; a run can hinge on getting a decent boss-killing gun and a second room-clearing gun
Many guns and items are considered weak or useless, and unlocked items still have to drop by chance
Limited variety in room layouts and enemy encounters; players who master it say rooms become memorisable and content after beating the Lich is sparse
Characters often feel similar, with some commonly described as near re-skins apart from special ones such as the Bullet and Robot
Normal rooms feel like a long runback to the boss fights; any damage taken in a boss fight (no-hit bonus) can feel demoralizing, and some reviewers call normal fights spammy or filler
Cryptic item descriptions and steep learning curve for newcomers
Some players report the camera/screen motion causes dizziness, high GPU usage, and an occasional co-op soft-lock with no settings fix
improvements: Add a way to ban or filter weak guns/items from the loot pool
More meaningful permanent progression or build-shaping choices at chests and shops
Online co-op (only local co-op exists), ideally with separate screens
More variety in room layouts, enemies and late-game challenge content
Camera and accessibility options (one reviewer reports motion-sickness dizziness and no fix in settings) and GPU usage tuning
More clarity on what unlocks and items do before selecting them
unique_things: Fully committed gun theme: floors, enemies, currency-like items and UI are all bullet or gun puns
Dodge roll with invincibility frames in a bullet-hell context, which divides hardcore shmup fans
Reward system for no-damage boss fights (extra heart containers/currency) that pushes skill play
Unusually large secret ecosystem: Rat fight, secret floors, secret NPC quests, alternate chambers, extra characters
Weapons with bizarre mechanics and references (for example a T-shirt cannon), with guns treated as characters
No permanent stat upgrades; progression is sideways, via unlocks, so skill remains the main variable
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding for the last unlockable characters and 100% achievements, including NPC quest chains that some find irritating (e.g. Frifle's quests, finding the Lost Adventurer)
Slow, sideways meta progression that never makes you stronger
Thieving rat stealing saved ammo, plus key and chest shortages frustrating runs
Runs ruined by ammo starvation or only having the starter pistol at the first boss
Long repetitive room-clearing stretches to reach the short, high-stakes boss fights
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans see it as fair and skill-based; others find it too punishing and unrewarding for those who struggle
RNG: some praise the huge synergy space, others say gear luck decides too much of each run
Dodge roll: loved for accessibility of movement, criticised by some bullet-hell purists as undercutting the genre
Content depth: fans cite hundreds of hours of secrets, while others say there is little post-game challenge and little run-to-run variety
community.reception_notes: Launch week sold over 200,000 copies (about 75% on Steam), 800,000+ by January 2017 and 3+ million across platforms by January 2020 (Wikipedia). SteamSpy lists 2-5 million Steam owners, and steam-revenue-calculator estimates roughly $67.6M gross and $20M net on Steam (Boxleiter-method estimate, not audited). Free content updates followed: Supply Drop (Jan 2017), Advanced Gungeons & Draguns (Jul 2018) and A Farewell to Arms (Apr 2019), after which development ended; some recent Steam reviewers note no updates since 2019. Critics at launch compared it favourably with The Binding of Isaac and Nuclear Throne, and PC Gamer called the bosses among the hardest things the reviewer had met. Nintendo Switch is the best-rated version on Metacritic (87); console reviewers noted controller aiming is less precise than mouse. A mobile release arrived in August 2025 and a 3D sequel, Enter the Gungeon 2, followed. Steam lists Windows and Linux, no native Mac. The 10th anniversary in April 2026 prompted renewed positive reviews.
